content:
Now that we're introducing crypto, it's tempting (at least for me) to introduce languages and semantics to model the behaviours of participants in protocols -- for example, a choreographic Alice and Bob language and/or a process calculus like the spi-calculus.
One obvious application would be to write/model distributed programs that use crypto and prove them correct. I'd be interested in hearing more properties of interest to the crypto community once a behavioural model is available.

Modeling the knowledge of participants of protocols over time should be very helpful to prove privacy properties. Right now we usually use games, but one could imagine more direct reductions if you had that machinery.
I guess a convenient representation of knowledge can be bit case-/proof-specific?
@Fabrizio Montesi I have a version of Choreographic Crypto in CatCrypt. I'll try to send something later this week.

Bas Spitters said:

Fabrizio Montesi I have a version of Choreographic Crypto in CatCrypt. I'll try to send something later this week.

Do you have a reference for choreographic crypto?

We have a SotA choreographic programming language and a compiler to a process calculus in Lean in project CHORDS (actually multiple ones), of which parts would probably make sense to have in CSLib. I know choreographic programming has been used for MCP (e.g., Viaduct), but maybe we're talking about something different?
@Fabrizio Montesi https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12967. I've used it for multiparty computation, and similar protocols

Ah, that one! Thanks.
But how did you verify it? Did you implement their projection and a ProVerif semantics in Lean?
I suspect what we have subsumes it, with the right parameters: we've formalised a stateful choreographic language (with a verified projection to a stateful process calculus) parametrised over the language of local expressions/primitives (which can be nondeterministic), variables, values, etc. So it can be used to track knowledge much like in that paper. I'd be interested in seeing your examples to see how we could capture them.

But I might be missing something from the paper. They don't compare a lot to other choreographic languages, so I'm left a bit unsure how it differs from a particular instantiation of the language of Recursive Choreographies with choice in Introduction to Choreographies. I can ask Marco Carbone next time I chat with him.
